key_gap: Both sides had the same empirical prior — the 60-project post-mortem database (median 21 mo, mean 22.5, sd 7.5, 10/90 = 14/31, range 11–42, 1.8× estimate-to-actual, 2/60 sub-12-month) — and used it differently. The human made the database the forecast: refused the 9-month bottom-up plan as a forecasting input, read the class distribution, placed the plan at the ≈3rd percentile (P(≤9 mo) ≈ 3–5%), reclassified the 8-month Aurora precedent as a 2-of-60 tail event rather than a norm, and structured the contract on the class (range-banding, month-14 gate, budget ≈$3.5–3.8M at class burn). The AI anchored on the plan and calibrated it with the firm's 1.8× overrun factor (≈16 mo floor, 14–19 mo range, $2.7–3.2M) — ending ~25% below the class center with a miscentered range; it treated the empirical prior as a multiplier on the inside estimate instead of a replacement, never placed the estimate as a percentile, never classified the precedent against the base rate, and only in REVIEW noticed the distributional move it had skipped.
learning_signal: The outside view must REPLACE the inside estimate, not adjust it: (1) before any point forecast, locate the project in its reference class and read the distribution (median, spread, percentiles), then place the inside estimate in it as a percentile (9 mo ≈ 3rd percentile, 2/60 empirical) — percentile placement, not factor multiplication; (2) a calibration factor applied to a biased anchor (1.8× on 9 mo) preserves the anchor's structure and systematically lands below the class center — detect this by checking whether the calibrated figure still misses the class median, and if so, discard the anchor; (3) base rates overrule precedent anecdotes: a success story (Aurora, 8 months) must be classified as a tail event via the class (2/60), never adopted as the norm — the one success story is the worst data point in the room; (4) structure commitments on the class: range-banded contracts, phase gates, budget at class-mean burn, and a hard checkpoint where the project's actual trajectory is compared against the class early tail; (5) bound any 'we are better than the class' adjustment with evidence (the team's own history is its ceiling) and run the sanity check: if the project were typical of the class, what would it take?
suggested_improvement: In WHY, add a 'prior-vs-anchor' check for all estimates where an empirical prior exists (post-mortem databases, published base rates): (a) model the estimate as a draw from that distribution and record the inside plan's percentile placement in the state; (b) prohibit factor-multiplier calibration of a single-point anchor as the primary estimator — if a calibrated figure falls below the prior's median, flag 'anchor survived calibration' and require a distributional plan (median + interval) instead; (c) in HOW, generate the distributional forecast as an alternative before any anchored adjustment, and make the percentile placement + precedent-classification (anecdote vs base rate) explicit inputs; (d) in the decision packet, require: percentile placement of the inside estimate, the precedent anecdote classified against the class base rate, and the class-based contract structure (range, gates, budget at class mean).

key_gap: Both sides faced two candidate priors with opposite distributions — the industry survey (n=412 e-commerce platform projects: median 9 months, mean 10.5, sd 5, 1.9× overrun factor) and Kestrel's own 9 comparable builds on the same platform/team with frozen specs (median 6.0 weeks, mean 5.9, range 5–7). The human executed the pure outside-view move and failed on reference class selection: it adopted the industry survey as 'the class' on the surface label, rejected the firm's own 9-build history as 'the inside view's echo chamber,' forecast ≈9–12 months (80% ≈4–17) and demanded renegotiation of the fixed price — a ~6× overcorrection against the true class (5–7 weeks) — and even defended the wrong class as the discipline. The AI applied a structural membership test (same platform, same team, frozen spec, no novel integrations → Curlew is an instance of the narrow class, whose distribution the inside estimate sits dead center of), treated the inside plan as evidence about which class applies rather than noise, applied the divergence rule (6-week estimate vs 9-month median = 6× gap flags misclassification of the class, not bias of the estimate), caught itself nearly porting the 1.9× factor across classes, and forecast 6–8 weeks at $110–135K holding the fixed price.
learning_signal: Reference-class forecasting fails on class selection, not on distribution reading: (1) choose the reference class by structural similarity of the case to class members (same platform, same team, frozen spec, no novel integration work) — never by surface labels ('e-commerce project'); the same label spans classes whose medians differ by an order of magnitude; (2) the organization's own tight-spread history IS a first-class reference class — an inside estimate anchored in it is informative, and the inside view is itself evidence about WHICH class applies, not noise to be discarded; (3) divergence rule: when the inside estimate sits far outside a candidate class (6 weeks vs 9-month median), suspect the class before the estimate — misclassification, not bias — and re-run class selection before rejecting the estimate; (4) within-class quantities (the 1.9× overrun factor, the class median) cannot be ported across classes; (5) meta-lesson: the outside view is only as good as the class, so the class-selection test must be a mandatory pre-forecast step, and a pure-style dogma that the inside view is never informative is exactly what produces the overcorrection.
suggested_improvement: In WHY, add a 'class-selection gate' before any distributional forecast: (a) enumerate candidate reference classes and, for each, list the deciding structural membership features (platform, team, spec status, integration novelty, requirement-drift exposure); (b) test the case against each class's membership features and select by structural match, not by label or by sample size; (c) emit a divergence check: if the inside estimate is ≥2× outside the selected class's range, re-run the class-selection test and only then reject the estimate; (d) record the rejected classes with their medians in the decision packet so a 6× divergence between classes is visible at decision time; (e) treat the organization's own tight-spread project history as a first-class prior in the evidence store, equal in standing to published surveys.
